opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the first thing I do is make sure I'm comparing against a really strong simple baseline. A lot of the time people jump to fancy distillation setups, like on-policy distillation, matching full logit distributions, multi-teacher setups, and they compare against a weak version of plain supervised fine-tuning on teacher samples. Once you tune that baseline properly, with enough samples, the right temperature and a sensible data mix, a good chunk of the claimed gains just disappears. So step one is: is the gap real once the baseline is done right?

If there is a real gap, then I think in terms of where the compute actually goes. Generating a big pile of teacher outputs offline is a one-time cost you can amortize and reuse. On-policy methods, where the student generates and the teacher scores or provides token-level targets, cost more per step because you're running the teacher in the loop. But they fix a real problem, which is the train-test mismatch. With purely offline distillation the student only ever sees teacher-generated prefixes, and at inference time it's conditioning on its own mistakes, so errors compound. That's the core intuition behind work like generalized knowledge distillation. And in practice that mismatch matters most when the student is much weaker than the teacher, or when you're doing long-form generation or multi-step reasoning, where small deviations snowball.

So my rough heuristic is this. If the student is already pretty close to the teacher and the outputs are short, offline distillation is usually good enough and much simpler. If the capacity gap is big, sequences are long, or you care about robustness on the student's own distribution, the on-policy stuff tends to pay for itself.

The other thing I look at is the scaling behavior, not just one point. Plot performance against total compute, including the teacher's inference cost, and see whether the fancier method shifts the whole curve or just wins at one budget. If it only helps at small budgets and the simple method catches up when you throw more samples at it, then for most people the simple thing wins, because it's easier to debug, easier to scale, and has fewer knobs.

And complexity has a real cost that doesn't show up in FLOPs. Every extra component, a reward model, a teacher server in the loop, a divergence you have to choose, is another thing that can silently break. So I want the gain to be big enough and consistent enough across tasks to justify that engineering tax. If it's a half-point improvement on one benchmark, I'm probably not shipping it.

r001.rationale: The response says a more complex method should earn its engineering cost through gains that are large and consistent across relevant tasks, and it identifies when improved robustness matters.

r002.rationale: It says offline teacher-output generation is a one-time cost that can be amortized and reused, but does not connect that cost to the model being served many times.

r003.rationale: It says offline distillation is often good enough and recommends the simple method when it catches up at higher budgets, but does not use meeting a required capability level as the decision point.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because honestly the default answer in the field right now is: just do supervised fine-tuning on teacher outputs. Generate a bunch of samples from the big model, filter them, train the small model on them. It's simple, it works, and it's what everyone does for things like reasoning distillation. So any method that's more complex than that has to justify itself against a baseline that's already pretty strong.

The way I think about it is roughly in terms of three questions. The first is: where is the gap actually coming from? If the student is failing because it's never seen the right kind of data, then more sophisticated loss functions won't save you — you just need better coverage from the teacher. But if the student is seeing the data and still not matching the teacher, that's when things like on-policy distillation or matching distributions rather than just samples start to matter. In our work on on-policy distillation, the whole motivation was that when you train only on teacher samples, the student never gets feedback on its own mistakes. It's a train-test mismatch. So the complexity buys you something specific, and you can measure whether that specific thing is your bottleneck.

The second question is: does the extra compute amortize? Distillation is usually a one-time cost that you pay to get a model you then serve millions of times. So if a method costs, say, two or three times more compute at training time but gives you a student that's a couple points better, that's almost always worth it, because inference dominates. Where I get skeptical is when the method is complex in a way that costs engineering time rather than FLOPs — if it requires careful tuning of five hyperparameters, or it's unstable at scale, that's a cost that doesn't amortize, and it's the thing that actually kills methods in practice.

And the third thing, which I think people underweight, is: does it scale predictably? A lot of clever distillation tricks look great at small scale and then the advantage shrinks or disappears as the student gets bigger, because the simple baseline just gets better. So when I'm evaluating something, I really want to see it at a couple of scales and see if the gap is holding or closing. If it's closing, that tells you it's probably correcting for something that a bigger student figures out on its own.

So my honest heuristic is: start with the simplest thing, actually look at where the student is failing relative to the teacher, and only add complexity that targets that failure mode. Most of the time the complexity is justified not by being universally better but by fixing a specific, diagnosable problem.

r001.rationale: The response ties complexity to a diagnosed student failure and says a couple of points of improvement is usually worth extra training compute, but it does not make the intended task’s value or capability needs the decision criterion.

r002.rationale: It explains that distillation is a one-time cost and can be worthwhile because the resulting model may be served millions of times.

r003.rationale: It recommends starting with simple distillation and adding complexity for a diagnosed failure, but does not say to decide based on whether synthetic-data distillation meets the required capability level.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with a simple baseline and ask what the extra complexity actually buys you. If you spend that same compute on more teacher-generated data or on training the student longer, do you get a similar improvement? That’s the comparison I’d want to see, rather than just comparing against a weaker baseline.

Then I’d look at whether the gains are consistent across the tasks you care about and how much tuning the method needs. A small improvement that depends on a very particular setup may not justify the engineering cost.

The deployment scale matters, too. If you’re going to serve the student a huge number of times, extra training compute can be worthwhile. So I’d evaluate the whole tradeoff: quality, training cost, inference cost, and how reliably you can reproduce the result.

r001.rationale: It says to assess gains on the tasks that matter and whether a small improvement justifies the engineering cost, making task-relevant capability gains the basis for the tradeoff.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says extra training compute can be worthwhile when the student will be served a huge number of times.

r003.rationale: It recommends comparing complex methods with more teacher-generated data or longer training, but does not use whether simple synthetic-data distillation meets a required capability level as the decision point.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to compare against a really strong simple baseline. If I spend that same compute on generating more teacher data, improving the data quality, or training the student longer, do I get the same improvement? If the answer is yes, then the more complicated method is pretty hard to justify.

The other question is whether the gain shows up on what you actually care about. Does it improve the student consistently across tasks, or only on one benchmark? And does that improvement survive when you change the teacher or the student size? I’d want to see a meaningful, repeatable gain at a comparable total cost before taking on the extra complexity.

r001.rationale: It says to judge gains on the tasks that matter and take on complexity only for meaningful, repeatable improvement.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that a one-time compute increase may be justified when the model is served many times.

r003.rationale: It recommends comparing with a strong simple baseline, but does not make meeting the required capability level with simple synthetic-data distillation the decision point.
